[THOUGHT]  
The patient presents with acute onset of pleuritic chest pain (worsens with inspiration), dyspnea, dry cough, fever, and fatigue — symptoms evolving over 5 days, with worsening respiratory and cardiac symptoms in the last 12 hours. Absence of risk factors for pulmonary embolism (no immobility, no leg symptoms, no personal/family history of VTE) and normal chest X-ray (no congestion, normal heart size) make heart failure or PE less likely. ECG findings — **sinus tachycardia, diffuse ST elevation, low-voltage QRS, and fluctuating R-wave amplitude** — are highly characteristic of **acute pericarditis**, especially when combined with **pericardial effusion on echocardiogram**. Pleuritic chest pain + fever + pericardial effusion + classic ECG changes strongly support **acute pericarditis**, likely viral (given subacute onset, systemic symptoms, absence of autoimmune or malignant history). Troponin may be mildly elevated (myopericarditis), but not yet reported. D-dimer, CRP, ESR, and serologies are pending but would further support inflammatory/infectious etiology.

[SUMMARY]  
**Clinical Impression:**  
✅ **Acute Pericarditis**, likely viral etiology (e.g., Coxsackievirus, SARS-CoV-2, EBV)  
— Supported by:  
 • Pleuritic substernal chest pain (worsens with inspiration)  
 • Acute-onset dyspnea and fever (5-day prodrome, acute decompensation in last 12 h)  
 • Classic ECG findings: diffuse ST elevation, sinus tachycardia, low-voltage QRS, oscillating R-wave amplitude  
 • Transthoracic echocardiogram confirming pericardial effusion  
 • Normal chest X-ray (no pulmonary congestion, normal cardiac silhouette)  
 • Absence of red flags for alternative diagnoses (no VTE risk factors, no history of heart/lung disease, cancer, or prior clots)  

⚠️ **Differential Considerations (less likely but to rule out):**  
- Myopericarditis (troponin pending)  
- Autoimmune pericarditis (ANA/RF pending)  
- Bacterial or tuberculous pericarditis (blood cultures, fluid analysis if large effusion)  
- Early STEMI (unlikely given diffuse ST elevation, lack of reciprocal changes, and pericardial effusion on echo)  

📌 **Next Steps Recommended (not stated but clinically indicated):**

- Check CRP and ESR (expected elevated in active pericarditis)  
- Viral serologies / PCR (SARS-CoV-2, EBV, Coxsackie)

The clinical summary presents a classic, textbook presentation of **acute pericarditis**: pleuritic chest pain, acute febrile illness with dyspnea, characteristic ECG changes (diffuse ST elevation, sinus tachycardia, low-voltage QRS, oscillating R-wave amplitude — the latter two being particularly suggestive of *significant pericardial effusion*), and echocardiographic confirmation of pericardial effusion. • Acute-onset dyspnea and fever with 5-day prodrome and decompensation in last 12 hours  
• Classic ECG findings: diffuse ST elevation, sinus tachycardia, low-voltage QRS, oscillating R-wave amplitude  
• Transthoracic echocardiogram confirms pericardial effusion  
• Normal chest X-ray (no pulmonary congestion, normal cardiac silhouette)
